latin: Fābriciō respondēre dēbeō. Habēsne<sup>1</sup> papȳrum<sup>2</sup>?
Hic est papȳrus! Vīsne ātrāmentum<sup>3</sup> et calamum<sup>4</sup>?
Grātiās: mihi est stilographium<sup>5</sup>. Incipiāmus<sup>6</sup>!
Mārcus Dupont Fābriciō Martinī<sup>7</sup> salūtem plūrimam dīcit!
Sī valēs bene est; ego valeō<sup>8</sup>!
Perlibenter<sup>9</sup> epistulam tuam acceptam lēgī<sup>10</sup>.
Tibi grātiās multās agō propter benignitātem tuam.
Adveniēmus Genuam diē 25° (vīcēsimō quīntō)<sup>11</sup> mēnsīs jūliī<sup>12</sup>, ad hōram nōnam antemerīdiānam<sup>13</sup>.
Cum gaudiō vōs revīsēmus et vōbīscum plūrēs diēs agēmus.
Salvē, optimē<sup>14</sup> Fābricī, valēte tū tuīque omnēs.
Scrībēbam Lutetiae Parīsiōrum, diē 19° (ūndēvīcēsimō) mēnsīs jūliī annō 1963° (mīllēsimō nongentesimō sexāgēsimō tertiō).
Epistulam in involūcrum īnserō. Īnscrīptiōnem scrībō. Pittacium conglūtinō et officium cursuāle petō.
latinAccented: Fābríciō respondḗre dḗbeō. Habḗsne<sup>1</sup> papȳ́rum<sup>2</sup>?
Hic est papȳ́rus! Vīsne ātrāméntum<sup>3</sup> et cálamum<sup>4</sup>?
Grā́tiās: mihi est stilográphium<sup>5</sup>. Incipiā́mus<sup>6</sup>!
Mārcus Dupont Fābríciō Mártinī<sup>7</sup> salū́tem plū́rimam dīcit!
Sī valēs bene est; ego váleō<sup>8</sup>!
Perlibénter<sup>9</sup> epístulam tuam accéptam lēgī<sup>10</sup>.
Tibi grā́tiās multās agō propter benignitā́tem tuam.
Adveniḗmus Génuam diē 25° (vīcḗsimō quīntō)<sup>11</sup> mēnsīs jū́liī<sup>12</sup>, ad hōram nōnam antemerīdiā́nam<sup>13</sup>.
Cum gáudiō vōs revīsḗmus et vōbī́scum plūrēs diēs agḗmus.
Salvē, óptimē<sup>14</sup> Fā́bricī, valḗte tū tuī́que omnēs.
Scrībḗbam Lutétiae Parīsiṓrum, diē 19° (ūndēvīcḗsimō) mēnsīs jū́liī annō 1963° (mīllḗsimō nongentésimō sexāgḗsimō tértiō).
Epístulam in involū́crum ī́nserō. Īnscrīptiṓnem scrībō. Pittácium conglū́tinō et offícium cursuā́le petō.
english: I must respond to Fabrizio. Do you have [some] paper?
Here-is [some] paper. Do you want ink and a quill?
Thanks: I have a pen. Let us begin.
Marc Dupont heartily salutes Fabrizio Martini (Marc Dupont to-Fabrizio Martini salute many-a he-is-saying).
If you are well (you-are-healthy), it is well; I am well (myself I-am-healthy).
I received and read your letter with great pleasure (most-gladly letter yours having-been-received I-read).
I thank you heartily for your kindness (to-you thanks many I-do on-account-of kindness yours).
We will arrive in Genoa on the 25th of July (day 25th of-month Julian) around 9 in the morning.
[It's] with pleasure [that] we will see you again and [that] we will spend several days with you.
Good-bye, excellent Fabrizio, be well (be-healthy) you and all of yours (yours-and all).
[Written] (I was writing) in [Paris] (Lutetia of the Parisians) on the 19th of July 1963 (day 19th of-month Julian year one-thousandth nine-hundredth sixtieth third).
I introduce the letter in an envelope. I write the address. I paste on the stamp and make for the [post] (postal) office.

footnotes: Habesne: it would be more classical to say estne tibi? Habeo (habes, habet, etc.) is used in general in senses rather different from those of our verb to have. It means more exactly to hold. For instance habere aliquem bonum, to hold somebody for good; or in lesson 13 (P 2): omnia male se habent.
Papyrum: formerly paper was made with the pulp of a reed called papyrus, hence its name. One can also say charta.
Atramentum, that which makes black. Ater (f. atra, n. atrum), means dark, matte black. Bright, shiny black is niger (nigra, nigrum).
Calamus, the reed or the quill. Perhaps you know (pink pages of the Larousse) the phrase lapsus calami, word-by-word: slip of the quill, i.e. a careless mistake.

Stilographium: the formation of this word is not very logical: stilus as well as graphium, both indicate the point to write on tablets (coated with wax). One could say, as do the English and Canadians: calamus fontanus, fountain pen.

Incipio, incipis, incipit, I begin, you…, etc. (present indicative). Incipiam, incipias, incipiat, incipiamus, incipiatis, incipiant, that I begin, that you…, etc., is the present subjunctive, used here instead of the imperative, which does not exist in the 1st person.

Marcus Dupont: the majority of first names have a well-defined Latin form, whereas last names are not always very easy to transpose. As a general rule one Latinizes only the first name. They do the same in French with foreign names: Marie (Mary) Stuart; Jules César, although in this last example Julius is not a first name. The person to whom we refer was actually called: Gaius (praenomen, first name) Julius (nomen gentilicium, name) Caesar (cognomen familiare, nickname: the curly).
The polite formula (P 5) is written in abbreviation: SVBEEV. Did you notice (thanks to plurimam) that salutem was feminine?

Perlibenter or libentissime are forms known as superlatives of the adverb libenter, gladly. These forms make it possible to show that the adjective or adverb is carried to its highest degree (very, the most, etc.).
Legi is the perfect of legere; present: lego, legis, etc.

Read the Latin figures well, but do not try to memorize them yet. Also think of reading those in the page and lesson numbers; when they will have become familiar to you, you will then be able to search for the missing ones, in the grammatical appendix.

Julius, is an adjective. Here it refers to mensis, the month, and because of this it becomes julii, because these two words form the possessive phrase from dié. Latin thinks: “in this 19th day of the month Julian”.
We have already seen (L 11, P 6) sextá horá (with a long á), at 6 o’clock. With the preposition ad, we use the form of the direct object, hence m’s of the endings that both these words take.

Optime is another superlative. As Latin does not use the polite form of you (fr. vous), it uses other means to mark a certain deference with regard to the person to whom one addresses oneself, and in particular the judiciously chosen superlative address. For instance if you write to a professor you can call him doctissime vir, very erudite man. For other professions, other terms could be more suitable: illustrissime, very famous; peritissime, very skillful, always followed by vir, man. In the feminine, replace the e with an a, and the vir with femina (doctissima femina, etc.). Why in the masculine is there an e and not an us? You will know soon.

latin: Difficile nōn est epistulam latīnam scrībere.
Īnscrīptiōne indicāmus cui hominī epistula perferrī dēbeat et in quō locō sit ejus domicilium.
Īnscrīptiō mea est: Carolus Durand 12 (in domō duodecimā), viā Lugdūnēnsī, Lutetiae Parīsiōrum, Galliā.
Ubi est officium cursuāle? Est in hāc viā.
Fābricius accēpit epistulam ā Carōlō scrīptam.
Epistulam tuam accēpī et eam libenter lēgī.
Quandō adveniētis? Adveniēmus diē septimō mēnsis jūniī.
Libenter vōs accipiēmus.
latinAccented: Diffícile nōn est epístulam latī́nam scrī́bere.
Īnscrīptiṓne indicā́mus cui hóminī epístula perférrī dḗbeat et in quō locō sit ejus domicílium.
Īnscrī́ptiō mea est: Cárolus Durand 12 (in domō duodécimā), viā Lugdūnḗnsī, Lutétiae Parīsiṓrum, Gálliā.
Ubi est offícium cursuā́le? Est in hāc viā.
Fābrícius accḗpit epístulam ā Carṓlō scrīptam.
Epístulam tuam accḗpī et eam libénter lēgī.
Quandō adveniḗtis? Adveniḗmus diē séptimō mēnsis jū́niī.
Libénter vōs accipiḗmus.
english: It is not difficult to write a (Latin) letter [in Latin].
By the address we indicate to-what person the letter must (debeat, subj.) be-taken and in what place his domicile is.
My address is Charles Durand, 12 Lyon Street (street Lyonian), Paris, France (Gaul).
Where is the post office? It is on this road.
Fabrizio received the letter written by Charles.
I received your letter and read it with joy.
When will you[pl.] arrive? We will arrive on the 7th of of June.
We will gladly receive you[pl.].
